title: 2 Samuel 15:30–37
context: David climbs the Mount of Olives weeping, head covered and barefoot, with the people mourning alongside him. Learning that Ahithophel has joined Absalom, David prays that God would turn Ahithophel's counsel into foolishness. At the summit, Hushai the Archite meets him, and David sends him back to Jerusalem to pose as Absalom's servant, defeat Ahithophel's counsel, and pass information through the priests.

verses.text: David went up by the ascent of the Mount of Olives, and wept as he went up; and he had his head covered and went barefoot. All the people who were with him each covered his head, and they went up, weeping as they went up.
verses.arminianNotes: David goes up the Mount of Olives weeping, barefoot, with his head covered. Arminian readers see deep repentance and grief, a king humbled by the consequences of his own sin and his son's betrayal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see David bearing God's discipline with humility. The scene of a weeping king ascending the Mount of Olives has led many to see a parallel with Christ's sorrow there, though the text does not draw it.

verses.text: Someone told David, saying, “Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom.” David said, “LORD, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness.”
verses.arminianNotes: "LORD, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness." Arminian readers see prayer as a real force in the story: David asks, and God will act through events in response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 2 Samuel 17:14 later says "the LORD had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel." David's prayer is answered through God's sovereign ordering of events.

verses.text: When David had come to the top, where God was worshiped, behold, Hushai the Archite came to meet him with his tunic torn and earth on his head.
verses.arminianNotes: At the summit "where God was worshiped," Hushai meets David in mourning. Arminian readers see God's answer to prayer arriving almost immediately, as a loyal friend appears at a place of worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God provides the means of answering David's prayer in the very next verse. God's providence often works through people who appear at exactly the right time and place.

verses.text: David said to him, “If you pass on with me, then you will be a burden to me;
verses.arminianNotes: David tells Hushai he would be a burden if he came along. Arminian readers note that David thinks strategically about how each friend can serve best, rather than simply gathering supporters around himself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see David discerning how to use the gifts God has given each person. Hushai's value lies not in fighting beside David but in a role only he can fill in Jerusalem.

verses.text: but if you return to the city, and tell Absalom, ‘I will be your servant, O king. As I have been your father’s servant in time past, so I will now be your servant; then you will defeat for me the counsel of Ahithophel.’
verses.arminianNotes: David asks Hushai to pretend loyalty to Absalom and defeat Ahithophel's counsel. Arminian readers note that the ethics of deception in war are debated, and that David sees this as resisting an unjust revolt.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also note the debated ethics of wartime deception. They point out that God uses Hushai's counsel to fulfill David's prayer (17:14), without the text pausing to evaluate the method.

verses.text: Don’t you have Zadok and Abiathar the priests there with you? Therefore whatever you hear out of the king’s house, tell it to Zadok and Abiathar the priests.
verses.arminianNotes: Hushai is to pass on what he hears to Zadok and Abiathar. Arminian readers see a network of faithful people working together, each taking real risks for the rightful king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God weaving together priests, a counselor, and their sons into a means of protecting his anointed. Providence works through coordinated human faithfulness.

verses.text: Behold, they have there with them their two sons, Ahimaaz, Zadok’s son, and Jonathan, Abiathar’s son. Send to me everything that you shall hear by them.”
verses.arminianNotes: Ahimaaz and Jonathan will carry the news to David. Arminian readers note that even the young men are called to courageous service, showing that faithfulness is not limited by age or position.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the sons of priests become messengers of deliverance. God uses the faithful households of Zadok and Abiathar to preserve the king he has chosen.

verses.text: So Hushai, David’s friend, came into the city; and Absalom came into Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: Hushai enters the city just as Absalom arrives. Arminian readers see the tension of timing: David's friend and his rebellious son reach Jerusalem at the same moment, setting up the coming contest of counsel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the precise timing as a mark of providence. God places Hushai in Jerusalem exactly when he is needed, preparing the way for Ahithophel's counsel to be overturned.
